old: the most trustworthy servant he had
new: the most thrifty servant he had
reason: Butler: "the swineherd, who was the most thrifty servant he had"; "trustworthy" replaces Butler's quality (careful husbandry, which the rest of the paragraph illustrates) with a different one.

old: it wouldn’t be right for me to turn him away
new: it wouldn’t be right for me to insult him
reason: Butler: "it would not be right for me to insult him"; turning a guest away is a different act from insulting him.

old: they sacrifice not just one victim but two
new: they sacrifice not just one or two victims
reason: Butler: "they sacrifice not one victim nor two only" (i.e. more than two); the draft says they sacrifice exactly two, reversing the sense of excess.

old: but you can still tell the grain from the straw that’s left
new: but if you look at the straw that’s left, you can still see what the grain was
reason: Butler: "if you look at the straw you can see what the ear was" (from what remains you can judge what I was); "tell the grain from the straw" is a different idiom, meaning to distinguish good from worthless.

old: the god soon robbed them of any chance
new: the god soon deprived them of any chance
reason: Butler's sentence is word for word the same as B12-P35 ("the god presently deprived them of all chance of getting home again"), which accepted Book 12 renders "the god soon deprived them of any chance"; the notes claim the formula was matched, but "robbed" diverges.

old: Odysseus had the sense to sit down
new: Odysseus was cunning enough to sit down
reason: Butler: "Ulysses was cunning enough to sit down"; "had the sense" drops the hero's defining trait of cunning.

old: May Zeus, my friend,
new: May Zeus, sir,
reason: Butler: "May Jove, sir, and the rest of the gods"; accepted Books keep Butler's "sir", and "my friend" is Butler's own words at ¶6, so two different forms of address collapse into one.

old: when they have young men for masters
new: when they have young lords for masters
reason: Butler: "when they have young lords for their masters"; "young men" drops the rank that makes the servants afraid.

old: Not a day or night passes but
new: Not a day or night comes from heaven but
reason: Butler: "Not a day or night comes out of heaven, but"; the image is dropped and the Book's "heaven" count falls from 6 to 5 (GLOSSARY hazard 5).

old: so instead of going home and courting his wife the proper way
new: so instead of going back to their own homes and making their offers of marriage in the usual way
reason: Butler: "they will not, therefore, go back to their own homes and make their offers of marriage in the usual way"; "his wife" is supplied and "usual" (custom) becomes "proper" (propriety).

old: either in Ithaca or on the mainland, was as rich as he was
new: either in Ithaca or on the mainland, is as rich as he was
reason: Butler: "No other great man ... is as rich as he was"; the present tense (no one now alive matches him) becomes a past comparison.

old: and Odysseus will never come home either way
new: nor will Odysseus ever come home
reason: Butler: "you will neither get paid for bringing good news, nor will Ulysses ever come home"; "either way" adds a sense of "regardless" that Butler does not have.

old: as the son of Cronus chooses to protect him or not
new: if the son of Cronus holds his hand over him to protect him
reason: Butler: "or else to escape if the son of Saturn holds his hand over him to protect him"; the image of the protecting hand is dropped and the condition is recast as a choice.

old: to me they gave only a small holding and little else
new: to me they gave a holding and little else
reason: Butler: "to me they gave a holding and little else"; "only a small" adds a size Butler does not state (GLOSSARY Voice and form, concrete detail).

old: It was then that Zeus turned his mind against me
new: It was then that Zeus planned evil against me
reason: Butler: "Then it was that Jove devised evil against me"; "turned his mind against me" softens the evil Zeus devises.

old: the gleam of bronze armor
new: the gleam of armor
reason: Butler: "with the gleam of armour"; "bronze" is a material Butler does not state.

old: as soon as we were well clear of Crete, with nothing to see but sky and sea,
new: as soon as we were well clear of Crete and could see nothing but sea and sky,
reason: Butler: "could see nothing but sea and sky" (here sea first; B12-P34 has "sky and sea", accepted as "could see nothing but sky and sea"); the draft reverses Butler's order and changes the construction of the recurring line (D29).

old: The gods, every one of them, must hate him
new: The gods, every one of them, hate him
reason: Butler: "The gods one and all of them detest him" is a flat assertion; "must" adds an inference hedge.

old: as a warning to tramps who go around the country telling lies
new: as a warning to tramps not to go around the country telling lies
reason: Butler: "as a warning to tramps not to go about the country telling lies"; Butler's deterrent (a warning not to lie) becomes a warning addressed to liars.

old: Then he stunned the pig with a length of oak he had kept back from the firewood,
new: Then he clubbed the pig with a length of oak he had kept back from the firewood and stunned it,
reason: Butler: "he clubbed the pig with a billet of oak ... and stunned it"; the blow itself ("clubbed") is dropped, softening the violence.

old: “Listen to me,” he said. “Eumaeus, and the rest of you. Once I’ve said a prayer,
new: “Listen to me, Eumaeus, and the rest of you,” he said. “Once I’ve said a prayer,
reason: Butler: "“Listen to me,” said he, “Eumaeus and the rest of you; when I have said a prayer…" is a split vocative, which PUNCTUATION §3 regroups; the draft's normalization leaves the vocative as a stranded fragment sentence.

old: and he was alert at once
new: and at once he was listening
reason: Butler: "and he at once gave me his ear"; being alert is not the same as listening to the speaker.

old: and everything in it has been quite satisfactory
new: and so far you have said nothing that is not quite satisfactory
reason: Butler: "have said nothing so far but what is quite satisfactory"; the hedge "so far" (Eumaeus taking the hint about the cloak) is dropped.

old: since heaven has kept from coming home the man who would always have been good to me and given me something of my own: a house, a piece of land, a good-looking wife, and everything else a generous master gives a servant who has worked hard for him and whose labor the gods have blessed, as they have blessed mine in the position I hold.
new: since heaven has kept from coming home the man who would always have been good to me. He would have given me something of my own by now: a house, a piece of land, a good-looking wife, and everything else a generous master gives a servant who has worked hard for him — for the gods have blessed my labor in the position I hold.
reason: One sentence stacks four or five levels of embedding (relative clause on "the man" -> a list introduced by a colon -> a relative clause on "servant" -> a further relative/comparative clause on "labor"). Heard aloud, a listener loses track of what "whose labor the gods have blessed, as they have blessed mine" attaches back to. Splitting after "good to me" and again before the final clause keeps every fact but removes the pile-up.

old: for I hate a man, as much as I hate the fires of hell, who lets his poverty tempt him into lying
new: for I hate a man who lets his poverty tempt him into lying as much as I hate the fires of hell
reason: The relative clause "who lets his poverty tempt him into lying" is separated from its noun ("a man") by the interjected comparison, so a listener briefly loses the thread of who is being described before the clause resolves. Moving the comparison to the end keeps noun and relative clause adjacent and reads the same way aloud.

old: hoping to wipe the house of Arceisius from memory in Ithaca
new: hoping to wipe the house of Arceisius—Odysseus’s grandfather—from memory in Ithaca
reason: "Arceisius" (Odysseus's grandfather) has not been introduced anywhere in the book; a first-time listener has no way to connect "the house of Arceisius" to Telemachus and his family, which is the point being made (the suitors want to end Odysseus's line by killing his son). The surrounding sentence still makes the stakes roughly clear, so this isn't fully blocking, but naming the family in terms already established (Odysseus) removes the guesswork. [lead: kept Butler’s name, added accurate brief gloss (Arceisius, father of Laertes) instead of replacing it]

old: my father, Castor son of Hylax—whose name I claim, a man held in the highest honor among the Cretans for his wealth, his prosperity, and the courage of his sons—treated me as an equal to my brothers born in wedlock.
new: my father, Castor son of Hylax, treated me as an equal to my brothers born in wedlock. It is his lineage I claim, and he was held in the highest honor among the Cretans for his wealth, his prosperity, and the courage of his sons.
reason: "My father, Castor son of Hylax—whose name I claim, a man held in the highest honor...—treated me..." stacks two parenthetical insertions onto "Castor" back to back ("whose name I claim" and "a man held in the highest honor..."), and "whose name I claim" reads ambiguously — a listener can't tell in the moment whether the speaker is claiming his father's name as his own or laying claim to something else. Dropping the ambiguous first insertion leaves a single, clear appositive and the sentence still establishes that the speaker uses his father's household name. [lead: keeps Butler’s “whose lineage I claim” (the proposal deleted it); the aside becomes its own sentence]

old: so much of it had he left in King Pheidon’s house.
new: he had left so much of it in King Pheidon’s house.
reason: "So much of it had he left" inverts subject and verb in a way that is grammatical but reads as period/poetic syntax rather than plain contemporary prose, and it's the only inversion of its kind in the book. Restoring normal word order ("he had left so much of it") removes the archaic stumble without changing the meaning.
